Beth Miller sits alone on a bench in a Port St. Lucie park, surrounded by trees, birds and the quiet sounds of nature.But for Beth, the stillness leaves plenty of room for memories.She comes here thinking about her daughter, Dawn, the daughter who once sat beside her in places just like this.WATCH THE STORY BELOW: Now, Beth is left searching for answers about how Dawn died — just hours after she was discharged from Cleveland Clinic Martin North Hospital following gallbladder surgery.Dawn Miller was admitted to Cleveland Clinic Martin North Hospital on Feb. Four days later, despite troubling symptoms, she was discharged. She died within hours of leaving the hospital."She went in for gallbladder surgery and she died four days later," Beth said.Dawn was 49 years old. She died two days before her birthday."Yeah, it's tough. We celebrate the day of her death, and then two days later we celebrate her birthday," said Beth. Medical records Beth shared with WPTV show Dawn was admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain. She underwent emergency surgery the following day, Feb. 25, 2024, to remove her gallbladder. Two days later, pathology confirmed she had gangrenous cholecystitis — a severe and life-threatening gallbladder condition.The post-operative report states Dawn "tolerated the procedure well," was returned to the recovery room in stable condition, and was later described as "alert, cooperative, and had no fever."The next day — Monday, Feb. 26 — records show Dawn's hemoglobin, a measure of red blood cells that carry oxygen, dropped.Clinical documentation shows a hospital employee sent a formal query the following afternoon — Feb. 27 — asking Dawn's doctor to confirm whether she had severe sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection in which the body starts damaging its own tissues.About an hour and 15 minutes later — at 1:24 p.m. — the response was sent back, checking the box next to "severe sepsis with acute lactic acidosis, present on admission." Underneath that, a notation states it was electronically signed by her doctor, who then ordered her antibiotics to be continued.Later that day, a doctor wrote in a hospital course note that Dawn's hemoglobin "was further low," noting she became "symptomatic": "pale and short of breath."Thirty minutes later, a nurse documented Dawn would "be discharged" that day, writing her vital signs were stable. But 90 minutes after that, another nursing note said Dawn declined discharge, telling staff she felt "weak" and "not ready" to go home.Beth described a phone call she received from Dawn that Tuesday night."She called me Tuesday night, and she was completely delirious. I couldn't understand a word she was saying, so my husband drove me down to the hospital. She was up all night screaming, I'm not going to die tonight," Beth said. She was burning up."Dawn's inpatient records show that overnight, she refused an antibiotic and underwent more bloodwork.At 8:56 a.m. the next morning — Wednesday, Feb. 28 — a hospital course note states Dawn again refused to leave the hospital, but that after speaking with a nurse, agreed to leave.Hospital records show Dawn's discharge was officially processed at 9:16 a.m. Beth says within minutes of getting home, her daughter collapsed."I couldn't get her up. I got her to crawl into the house, and she belly flopped onto the sofa," Beth said.A nursing note states Beth watched her daughter go into cardiac arrest and immediately started CPR."Panic, complete panic. And I was alone," Beth said. "I was calling 911, and they were telling me to roll her on the floor and start giving her chest compressions.""And I just felt so helpless, you know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening, and it seemed like it was forever that the Fire Rescue didn't get there and she was just laying there," Beth said. "She was dead about 10 or 15 minutes later."By 10:40 that morning, emergency records show Dawn was back at Cleveland Clinic Martin North with no pulse. Staff immediately began chest compressions, but at 11:11 a.m., she was pronounced dead.Beth said she immediately requested an autopsy."A bunch of people wandered in and out to say how sorry they were. And I demanded an autopsy. And they said, that's not a problem. We'll give you an autopsy. We'll get her an autopsy," Beth said.Records back that up. Two nurses documented that Beth requested an autopsy before Dawn was sent to the morgue.But hours later, a nurse manager wrote that "the medical examiner released the body" and "was not requiring an autopsy."The note states Beth remained "adamant that she wants an autopsy completed" — but was told the hospital "could not make that decision" and that her request "would be documented in the chart that she was requesting the autopsy but could not pay.""She never got an autopsy," Beth said.Records show that by 12:30 that afternoon, hospital staff had already contacted LifeLink Tissue Bank in Tampa. By that evening, Dawn's body was removed from the hospital for an off-site tissue donation, with records stating the "body will not return to the hospital.""I couldn't believe it. They had to put her — as soon as we left, they sent her to Tampa. There was nothing," Beth said.In a clinical note written after Dawn's death, the attending physician said he suspected she suffered a massive cardiac arrest. After he "reviewed her records," he said she "had normal chemistries" — but made no note of the cholecystitis diagnosis, the sepsis query, or the drop in hemoglobin.Dr. Gerald Feigin, a forensic pathologist and medical examiner who has spent more than 40 years performing autopsies in New Jersey, reviewed Dawn's medical records."I've done over 25,000 [autopsies] in my career," Feigin said.When asked whether Dawn's chemistries were normal, as per the assessment of the attending physician, his response was direct."No, absolutely not, because they're not normal," Feigin. "Looking at the CBC, the blood count, that wasn't normal."Feigin was referring to bloodwork taken five hours before her discharge on Feb. 28 — labs marked "abnormal," with at least eight components flagged as either high or low. A basic metabolic panel taken at the same time was also marked "abnormal," and Feigin said those results indicated low kidney function."Her kidney function went right down. So it was not good," Feigin said.Feigin was most concerned about the drop in Dawn's hemoglobin. Though records show her doctor ordered a blood transfusion the day before discharge, by the next morning her hemoglobin had risen slightly — but only to 8.2. The Cleveland Clinic's own website states a hemoglobin below 12 in women is "a severe low level," meaning her body wasn't getting enough oxygen."That's a red flag. People are weak after surgery, but don't — I mean, the hemoglobin dropping that rapidly, that's a red flag. I mean, that's glaring," Feigin said.When asked directly whether Dawn should ever have been discharged, Feigin did not hesitate."No, absolutely not," Feigin said. "When somebody's losing hemoglobin that rapidly, you better figure out why, and they shouldn't be discharged."Feigin also addressed the cardiac arrest Dawn suffered within hours of leaving the hospital."Absolutely," Feigin said when asked whether it was likely tied to the conditions documented in her records. "But that's why you do an autopsy. The hospital should have done an autopsy, plain and simple." Cleveland Clinic was contacted for comment. The hospital said it could not comment because it is bound by patient privacy laws. When asked to explain its discharge policies and when an autopsy should be performed, the hospital again declined to answer those questions or address Feigin's concerns.Dawn's treating physicians were also contacted — including the doctor who discharged her, her attending physician, and the emergency physician who pronounced her dead and reviewed her lab results. None responded to our calls or emails requesting an interview.Records from the Florida Department of Health show no public complaints or disciplinary actions against any of the doctors involved. Additional records from the Agency for Health Care Administration show no disciplinary action against the hospital.Feigin makes it clear: we will never know for certain whether Dawn would have survived, or what ultimately caused her death. "It's on your mind, 24/7," Beth said. It will always be difficult. I see her laying on that floor all the time." But even if Beth had those answers, her legal options would be limited under Florida's Free Kill law — specifically, state limits on who can sue for wrongful death. That will be the focus of WPTV's follow-up investigation.If you have had a similar experience, we invite you to share it with us.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A body was found following an extensive search in Martin County, but the sheriff's office could not confirm whether it was that of a man reported missing Aug. On Tuesday, the Martin County Sheriff's Office announced that a body had been recovered from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge. Budensiek said investigators later found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search. Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to a body. Budensiek said. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found.

Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is investigating after a man said he shot a dog because the animal charged at his wife and him on Sunday in the Indian River Estates subdivision. Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage and conducting interviews with independent witnesses and gathering additional information about the incident. The shooting occurred in the 5900 block of Palm Drive in Fort Pierce. According to a preliminary investigation, the woman pulled into her driveway, and two dogs approached her vehicle and prevented her from safely getting out of her vehicle. She contacted her husband for assistance. He said he came outside and observed the dogs before returning inside the residence to retrieve a handgun. When he came back outside, one dog charged toward him in an aggressive manner, the sheriff's office said. As the dog approached and before he was bitten, the man fired his handgun, striking one of the dogs. After the shooting, both dogs fled to a nearby residence on Myrtle Drive, where they reside. The owner transported the injured dog to an emergency animal hospital for treatment. The dog’s condition is not currently available. "At this time, the investigation remains active, and no further conclusions will be drawn until all available evidence has been reviewed," the sheriff's office said. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office remains committed to conducting a thorough and objective investigation and will provide additional verified information when appropriate." At least five people are dead after an Amazon cargo aircraft overran the runway during a landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles on a road surrounding the airport, officials said.There is no apparent threat to public safety at this time, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said during a news conference Sunday evening. The scene is still active.“Units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” an X post from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue says.More than 60 fire units responded to the scene to put out the fire, a spokesperson for Miami-Dade Fire Rescue told CNN.“We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to CNN. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened.”“Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected,” the statement continued.The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and landed on runway 30, which is more than 9,000 feet long, according to FAA data.The National Transportation Safety Board said it is gathering information about the crash and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate.It’s not clear why the plane was unable to stop before the end of the runway. A review of air traffic control audio by CNN shows the pilots did not declare an emergency before the landing.Later, inspection crews reported there were no aircraft parts or debris found on the runway, but the plane damaged navigational equipment when it left the pavement.A ground stop at the airport was lifted around 5 p.m. ET, and there’s a ground delay into Monday due to the disabled aircraft on the runway, according to the FAA.The FAA said the 21 Air flight overran the runway around 2 p.m. The airline is a cargo carrier with an operations center in Miami that performs flights for companies like Amazon and DHL using Boeing 767 aircraft.Runway excursions – when airplanes go off the runway – are the number one incident involving airplanes worldwide, according to data from the International Air Transport Association.The runways at Miami International, like many airports, have a designated safety area that serves as a buffer in case excursions occur.CNN’s Sarah Dewberry and Nayeli Jaramillo-Plata contributed to this report.The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

Kids are coming alive in ways that are transforming the campus for the better," Glick said.Not every student was on board at first. Senior Chloe Caraffa said the adjustment was not easy."Getting something taken away from you that was once really accessible your senior year...you're not really feeling it," Caraffa said.But after just a few days, Caraffa said she noticed a change in her own behavior."I have been so much more social with other people. I find myself going up to people and talking instead of texting them on my phone," Caraffa said.She also said the policy revealed something about her study habits."I used to complain about staying up late and how much homework I had, and the reality is my phone was the problem," Caraffa said.The school wants parents to know that if there is an emergency and they need to reach their child, they can contact the school directly.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Vero Beach woman is being held without bond on two sexual battery charges after an Internet Crimes Against Children investigation in Michigan led deputies to her Indian River County home, according to an arrest affidavit. Lisette Zamarripa, 28, was arrested Sept. 3 by the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office . She is charged with two counts of sexual battery and one count of electronic transmission of child sexual abuse material. Zamarripa’s arraignment is scheduled for 9 a.m. According to the affidavit, Michigan State Police received a National Center for Missing and Exploited Children cybertip involving alleged child sexual abuse material associated with a Kik account. Investigators obtained a search warrant for the account and found images and videos allegedly showing an adult woman engaging in sexual acts with two children, a 1-year-old girl and a 2-year-old boy, both her biological children. DCF took custody of the children. Michigan investigators identified the woman as Zamarripa after comparing material from the account with her Facebook profile, the affidavit states. Michigan investigators also served a search warrant on Zamarriapa's boyfriend, Kenneth Conkle, where he admitted to directing and recording the abuse. He confessed to separately abusing his own 1-year-old daughter. Indian River County deputies went to Zamarripa’s Vero Beach home after investigators believed the children could be in immediate danger. A family member confirmed Zamarripa was inside with her two children, according to the affidavit. Deputies said Zamarripa came outside with the children and was separated from them. After being advised of her rights, she allegedly admitted that she committed sexual acts involving both children during a FaceTime call with their biological father, who lives in Michigan. He faces charges in Michigan including child sexual battery, four counts of production of aggravated CSAM, and five counts of using a computer to commit a crime. Florida charges against Conkle are pending. The affidavit says Zamarripa told detectives the acts had been discussed with the father beforehand and that she livestreamed at least one incident for him to view. Investigators said she initially denied one allegation but later identified the children in sanitized images shown to her and admitted the conduct described in the evidence. See also: Florida woman cleared under 'Stand Your Ground' after deadly Walmart parking spot fight Deputies seized Zamarripa’s cellphone, which she allegedly said was used to record the material. She is being held with no bond on the two sexual battery charges. Bond was set at $500,000, cash or surety, on the electronic transmission charge. The affidavit states prosecutors intended to seek a grand jury indictment on two counts of capital sexual battery because of the children’s ages.

Youth hockey players from across South Florida got the chance to skate where the Florida Panthers practice this weekend, as Florida Panthers star Matthew Tkachuk hosted his hockey celebration tournament at the Baptist IcePlex in Fort Lauderdale.Tkachuk partnered with Baptist Health to create the tournament at the end of summer — a nod to his own days as a young player.WATCH: Matthew Tkachuk hosts youth hockey tournament to inspire new players"This exact weekend was always the weekend that I started like my tournaments and that was always the most exciting for me because you got to kick it off. "Oh my gosh, it's the best sport in the world," Tkachuk said.Tkachuk said expanding hockey's reach in South Florida has been a priority since joining the Panthers."Obviously my number one goal was coming down here to win a championship and right behind that was I really wanted to see hockey grow here," Tkachuk said.All weekend, families visited the IcePlex to test their slap shot, and some learned how to play for the first time with Tkachuk's help. Indiantown's new interim village manager is speaking out for the first time about how he plans to lead the village following a surprise appointment that came just one week after he lost his job as Stuart city manager.Michael Giardino was named interim village manager Tuesday after the Indiantown Village Council voted to terminate former Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, with some council members citing no confidence. The move came as residents packed the council meeting, urging more transparency about plans for data centers."Transparency is the Hallmark of governance," Giardino said.Giardino addressed his approach to the role, signaling a shift in direction for village leadership."I do things ethically, morally, and in accordance with the law and I believe this council wants to do the same and they heard their constituents loud and clear and so that's the way we'll move forward," Giardino said.Three new council members were elected after ousting incumbents in the last election. Resident Kimberly Jackson Brown said the change in management was a welcome one."It was a step in the right direction because the previous council had lost the trust of the people," Jackson Brown said.Resident Eric Miller echoed that sentiment."The outcome is to be applauded because those people made some pretty big moves yesterday and did it for the right reasons, not out of spite—they did it because they're acting as good Americans in an elected role," Miller said.Giardino said his appointment came after council members reached out to him following his departure from Stuart."I was invited to come by a few of the council members. They knew my circumstance and they were curious and interested, so I was there and I answered their calls," Giardino said. "Being received here in Indiantown, it's a joy and could have been destiny all along."The Navy veteran points to his experience running commercial airports as evidence he is prepared for the position."It is running a small city. The budgeting is the same, the personnel matters are the same, the things that you concentrate on are just about the same," Giardino said.While residents say they are cautiously optimistic, Jackson Brown made clear that accountability will be expected."He needs to know that if he–if he doesn't take instruction from the council as council takes instruction from the people then he can go to," Jackson Brown said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie man is accused of striking the mother of his children with a vehicle and driving several houses down the street while she was on the hood, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Brandon Isaiah Martin, 24, was arrested Sept. 2 on an outstanding warrant charging him with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. The warrant identifies a motor vehicle as the alleged weapon. The charge stems from an April 28, 2025, incident on 26th Court Southwest in Vero Beach, court records show. Deputies said the woman went to the home after a friend told her Martin was there removing property. The woman told deputies Martin was attempting to leave with their two children. The pair had joint custody but no formal custody documentation, according to the probable cause affidavit. As the woman was placing one of the children into another vehicle, Martin allegedly drove a silver Kia Soul toward her and struck her, causing her to land on the hood, deputies wrote. The woman told deputies Martin continued driving with her on the hood for about four or five houses. She said she heard him threaten to kill her, according to the affidavit. The vehicle stopped after Martin’s mother, who was in the front passenger seat, put it in neutral, deputies said. The woman was able to get off the hood and told deputies she feared for her life. A witness told deputies she saw Martin drive toward the woman, strike her and continue down the street with the woman still on the hood. Deputies documented abrasions to the woman’s knees, records show. See also: Florida woman cleared under 'Stand Your Ground' after deadly Walmart parking spot fight A judge approved the warrant May 5, 2025, and set Martin’s bond at $50,000. The order also prohibits him from contacting the woman and requires him to stay specified distances away from her, her home, workplace and vehicle. Deputies served Martin with the warrant at a Vero Beach address on Sept. Jail records show he later posted bond.

Linn Stewart, a 75-year-old resident of Indian River County, starts her day at 2:30 a.m., driving through the dark to feed her colony of stray cats, a routine that has become central to her life. "You're up at 2:30 every morning?" she was asked. "Umm hmm, a lot of times I'm out at 2:30 every morning," Stewart said. While most people are still asleep, Stewart is already hard at work caring for animals that have become like family to her. "I've only required four hours of sleep since I was little. I drove my parents crazy," she said. Her love for animals has been a lifelong passion. "I've always loved animals. I would bring home anything and everything," Stewart said. "Once I got involved with (For the Love of) Paws, I realized that there were so many cats running around that I would just take care of them." After feeding the cats, Stewart volunteers 60 hours a week at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere, a sanctuary for pets left behind by senior citizens who can no longer care for them. The organization also operates a pet food pantry, providing free pet food to food banks, veterans, and senior citizen organizations. "We have a cat group and a dog group, and we put them on the tables, and we cut open the bags and dump them in bins, and then what we do is we transfer them to 4-pound bags," Stewart said. Stewart said the sanctuary provides more than just food. We provide medical sometimes. We get the donations and provide flea medications if we have it. It's just something that is really needed and appreciated," she said. Having lost her parents at the age of 30 and with little family nearby, Stewart said giving back is what keeps her going. I would be finding something to do," she said. Her compassion extends beyond cats and dogs. "I've stopped and rescued tortoises, turtles. I stopped one time last week, there was a coyote that had gotten hit. I realized it was a coyote. I still called to have somebody pick it up," she said. Stewart’s dedication has not gone unnoticed. "Love for Paws is part of your family. Well, at Guardians, we live that as well. We'd like to welcome you to the Guardians family, and thanks for all you do. You're rooted in your community, and we love to celebrate that. So congratulations, $525.25 goes to you," she was told. For Stewart, her work is a source of purpose and joy. "It keeps me going," she said. "I'll probably just disappear one day, but other than that, I have no health issues right now. Knock on wood, but this keeps me going because I have love for the animals." If you live in Indian River County or are just passing through, don’t be surprised if you see Stewart lending a hand to the helpless. WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end the year, bringing to a close her seven-plus years at the helm of the league and a stewardship that has been transformative and at times tumultuous.Engelbert is the second-longest tenured WNBA president or commissioner, and she helped negotiate a lucrative collective bargaining agreement this past spring that resulted in the league's first set of million-dollar player salaries."Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league's 30-year history," NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said Friday when announcing Engelbert's decision. "We are grateful for Cathy's leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women's basketball."Engelbert, who turns 62 in November, told The Associated Press that she has been thinking about retiring for months.RELATED STORY | WNBA to discuss transgender athlete policies at league meetings"When I first came to the league I intended to do this for 3 1/2 years," she said in a phone interview. "The 7 1/2 years exceeded that time. This is a really good time given the financial transformation journey we've been on. Getting the collective bargaining agreement done, getting a long-term media rights deal done, getting expansion done."Engelbert insists that the decision to leave was solely her own and that she did not feel any pressure to step down from NBA or WNBA stakeholders.Engelbert: Several unidentified successors on league's radarThe commissioner said she has been working on a succession plan over the last few years. While she didn't give any specifics on who might be considered for the position, Engelbert did say there are both internal and external potential candidates on the league's radar."It's a good time to hand it off to the next leader to take the 'W' into a better phase," she said. "I'm proud of the team we built and everything we accomplished. A leader knows when it's time to drop the mic and move on after building a powerhouse team in the league office."Engelbert said she has mixed emotions about leaving."I love women's basketball and am not going anywhere yet. We'll run a real succession process in the remaining four months. If we don't find someone I'll stay on," she said. I walked in the door and I was by myself as no one transitioned me into this role."Hopefully I can help this next leader transition in especially considering the elevation of this league."The WNBA has grown at an exponential rate during Engelbert's tenure as commissioner, with record television ratings, strong attendance, a new long-term media rights deal and expansion to 18 teams by the end of the decade."I was brought in as a business leader to transform the business," she said. "I look at revenue and merchandise, viewership and attendance," she said, noting how they've all improved. "A great leader senses when it's time for someone else to come in. When I came in, this league was facing questions about our long-term viability and sustainability."Engelbert said the growth of the league has "blown away her expectations" since she stepped into her role after leaving her previous position as president of Deloitte in 2019.Besides the new CBA, the list of things she is most proud of includes getting charter travel for players, keeping the league going during the coronavirus pandemic, the historic media rights deal and exponential increase in the value of of WNBA franchises. In 2019, the average value of a WNBA franchise was $10 million; in 2026, it is about $460 million.Along with the financial gains, however, turmoil and tension have accompanied the WNBA's growth.Players say they have seen more social media vitriol directed toward them over the last few years and some don't feel the league has done enough to ensure their safety. The league also has been at the center of discussions about transgender athletes playing in the league.Engelbert has repeatedly said the online attacks of players are unacceptable and she backs league initiatives to protect players. She also said there should be no confusion on the transgender question."We have no current eligibility issues in the WNBA," Engelbert said, adding that "if we did, we would have a thoughtful policy discussion with the (players' association) and the players."While there was a strained partnership between the commissioner and players during the recent CBA negotiations, Engelbert insists she has a good relationship with them.Talks between the commissioner and players have been complicated.RELATED STORY | WNBA growth amplifies longstanding debates over race, gender and powerNew York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart, vice president of the WNBA players' union executive committee, said before the All-Star Game that there is a respect for Engelbert among the players, just not much of a relationship.Engelbert said she is ready to do what most retirees plan: spend more time with family.She also admitted that the online hate she receives has affected her family as well, though she did not share details of the impact."There have been some hard parts of that on my family with the vitriol and hate I get online," Engelbert said.Her retirement will make her mother happy."My mom is turning 90 this year, and she said that 'it would be good if you were retired to spend more time with me,'" Engelbert said, laughing. "I have two children, one I barely see."I'm one of eight kids (and I) have five brothers. They always say can you retire so you can spend more time with us."Come Jan. 1, her family will get its wish.

Lucie County could become a data center, according to a rezoning application sent to the city of Fort Pierce.Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center.WATCH BELOW: New 203-acre data center proposed in St. Lucie CountyThe rezoning application said, "the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial."Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area."You have a beautiful view all the time," Whiteside said.When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate."I hate that idea," Whiteside said.The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project."He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said.Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system.According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food."Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions."Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said.Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution."If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said.The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. According to the application, "the partner company would need to submit to the City a site plan application for the proposed data center and obtain City approval of the site plan."The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board on Sept.

Less than a year after JetBlue touched down at Vero Beach Regional Airport, the airline is already cutting one of its routes. Starting Wednesday, September 9, JetBlue will permanently end flights from the Vero Beach Regional Airport to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. In a statement obtained by CBS12 in July, the airline said demand for the route has not materialized as the company had hoped, but it will continue to serve Vero Beach through Boston. JetBlue said customers who booked flights were notified directly and were issued a refund to their original form of payment. This comes as JetBlue adds eight new nonstop routes to Fort-lauderdale Hollywood International Airport. Kennedy International Airport and Boston Logan International Airport. hero.headline: JetBlue ends Vero Beach-to-JFK route Sept. 9 after demand falls short
hero.body:
JetBlue permanently ended flights from Vero Beach Regional Airport to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday, September 9, less than a year after the route launched. The airline said demand for the route has not materialized as the company had hoped. The decision comes after the airport invested about $5 million in construction projects for baggage claim and covered walkways tied to the new JetBlue service.

JetBlue will continue serving Vero Beach through Boston Logan International Airport. Customers who booked flights on the JFK route were notified directly and were issued a refund to their original form of payment, according to a statement the airline provided to CBS12 in July.

JetBlue announced in December 2025 that it would begin serving Vero Beach Regional Airport with daily flights to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport and Boston Logan International Airport. The airport expected the new service to bring an influx of passengers, prompting the infrastructure improvements.

The route cancellation comes as JetBlue adds eight new nonstop routes to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport.

hero.headline: Ex-Fort Pierce officer jailed on $80K bond for 400+ database searches on ex
hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond after being charged with four felonies for allegedly misusing police databases to track an ex-girlfriend. Fort Pierce police Chief David Smith announced Tuesday that Crutchfield conducted more than 400 searches to monitor a single vehicle between October 2022 and July 2023.

Crutchfield used four different police databases to track the vehicle, including Flock cameras 382 times, which allowed him to monitor the victim's location and movements, according to the police report. The registered owner of the vehicle was an ex-girlfriend. Most of the queries were made when Crutchfield was off duty, Smith said.

"Conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach in the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. Crutchfield resigned from the department in August shortly after learning he was under investigation.

Smith called the arrest "a black eye" for the department but said investigators had an obligation to act when credible evidence suggested an officer may have violated the law. "The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," Smith said. The chief announced changes to department policies regarding police database access, limiting who can access them and requiring permission from a deputy chief for all searches.

hero.headline: Martin County celebrates completion of C-23 Canal water diversion project
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis visited Martin County to celebrate the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project, a multimillion-dollar initiative designed to improve water quality in the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River while supporting water levels in Lake Okeechobee. Since operational testing began in May, the project has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water into its system to treat, store, and move clean water back into local communities.

DeSantis joined officials from the South Florida Water Management District for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to mark the occasion. The project, which has been years in the making, aims to clean up pollution in these major waterways.

The C-23 Canal project will divert harmful discharges from the canal in St. Lucie County and redirect the water south to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area in Martin County. Once there, the water can be treated before being released into the St. Lucie River.

The goal is to reduce harmful discharges and algal blooms in the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon. DeSantis highlighted the project's progress during the ceremony, noting the nearly 5 billion gallons already diverted through the system for treatment and storage.

hero.headline: 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District moves forward in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
An 85-acre entertainment district is moving forward in the Tradition community of Port St. Lucie, with the first phase already 60 percent leased and construction expected to begin within six months. The Tradition Entertainment District will bring new restaurants and retail along Village Parkway between Innovation Way and Hegener Drive.

Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, said the first phase will develop a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way with 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said he plans to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The retailers are eager to open, according to Lumer.

The development is divided among four parcels. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the hub of the entertainment district, with plans for potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater. Visitors will be able to park or arrive by golf cart and spend the afternoon visiting different places, Lumer said.

Lumer said the district will help keep and attract business to Port St. Lucie. Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often. Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need for more places where people can intermingle on a regular basis. Lumer said developers are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

The development is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Lumer said he hopes to bring in around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. “There’s a need for diversity, and they keep telling us that they want different options,” Lumer said. hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer faces felony charges for tracking ex-girlfriend
hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield is scheduled to appear in court Wednesday on four felony charges for allegedly misusing law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend. Police say Crutchfield searched his ex-girlfriend's vehicle in the department's Flock license plate reader system 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026 without a legitimate law enforcement reason. Investigators say Crutchfield also used other police databases to search for personal information.

Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave in August and later resigned from the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Fort Pierce police have tightened access to the Flock system and started a broader audit of department databases. The chief says no other violations have been found so far.

Police say Josepher Crutchfield searched his ex-girlfriend’s vehicle in the department’s Flock license plate reader system 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026 without a legitimate law enforcement reason. Investigators say Crutchfield also used other police databases to search for personal information. He was placed on administrative leave in August and later resigned from the department. Crutchfield now faces four felony charges related to unauthorized computer access. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Fort Pierce police have since tightened access to the Flock system and started a broader audit of department databases. Now, the chief says a departmentwide audit is underway, and so far, no other violations have been found. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teacher uses survivor accounts to teach 9/11 to students born after attacks
cards.teaser: Ayleen Charles, a social studies teacher at Sunlight Christian Academy in Port St. Lucie, dedicates time each September to teaching students about the September 11 attacks through firsthand survivor stories and voicemails left by passengers.
cards.body:
Ayleen Charles, a social studies teacher at Sunlight Christian Academy in Port St. Lucie, makes September 11 a centerpiece of her classroom each fall. Charles, who has taught at the school for nearly a decade, uses survivor stories, images, and audio recordings to help students understand a day they never lived through.

Charles said her students have only known a world shaped by the attacks. To make the history feel real, she shares firsthand accounts from those who were there, including voicemails left by people on the airplanes. Charles said she wants to show students the realness of what happened, not just something printed in a history book.

Part of the lesson includes explaining how everyday life changed after the attacks. Charles said students are shocked when she tells them people used to be able to pass through what is now TSA security and watch airplanes take off from the gate. The lessons also cover how the nation came together after the tragedy.

Charles said the responsibility to remember will be carried forward by the students she teaches. She wants them to understand how the attacks impacted the people they know and the world they live in today. For Charles, the mission is personal. She said the people who lost their lives because of an act of hatred deserved to be remembered, and their legacy deserved to be carried on.

Charles said.Charles said her students have only ever known a world shaped by the attacks."You were born in a world shaped by 9/11. hero.headline: Palm City C-23 canal diversion project complete after $57 million, 3.5-year build
hero.body:
The C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project is now complete in western Palm City. Gov. Ron DeSantis joined the Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and the Executive Director of the South Florida Water Management District at a ribbon-cutting Wednesday afternoon to mark the completion of the $57 million project, which took about three and a half years to build.

The project features a nearly 7-mile canal and pump station designed to divert excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the St. Lucie Estuary and into the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area, where it will be treated before entering the estuary. The infrastructure aims to improve water quality and bring the flow of the St. Lucie Estuary closer to its natural pattern, DeSantis said.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer charged with felonies for tracking ex-girlfriend with police databases
hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond after being charged with four felonies for allegedly misusing police databases to track an ex-girlfriend.

Fort Pierce police Chief David Smith said Tuesday that Crutchfield used four different police databases to monitor a single vehicle from October 2022 to July 2023. Crutchfield conducted more than 400 searches, using Flock cameras 382 times, which allowed him to track the victim's location and movements, according to the police report. The registered owner of that vehicle was an ex-girlfriend.

"Most of these queries were made when he was off duty," Smith said. "Conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach in the trust that's placed in law enforcement."

Crutchfield resigned from the department in August shortly after learning he was under investigation, Smith said.

"This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community," Smith said. He called the arrest "a black eye" for the department but emphasized investigators did what had to be done.

"When there is credible evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," Smith said.

Smith announced changes to department policies regarding police database access, limiting who can access them and requiring permission from a deputy chief for all searches.

hero.headline: C-23 diversion project in Palm City now operational, rerouting billions of gallons from St. Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
A new water management project in Palm City is redirecting billions of gallons of water away from the St. Lucie Estuary to reduce the risk of harmful algal blooms. Governor Ron DeSantis joined state environmental officials in Palm City on Wednesday to mark the completion of the C-23 Estuary Discharge Diversion Project, which entered operational testing in May and has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water.

The project includes nearly seven miles of new canal and a pump station that redirects excess water from the C-23 Canal to the C-44 reservoir and stormwater treatment area. Drew Bartlett, executive director of the South Florida Water Management District, said the pump station can move as much as 166 million gallons of water per day. The system has worked since May 14, according to Bartlett.

Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the completed project is expected to divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the St. Lucie Estuary annually. The project is also projected to prevent an average of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the river each year. Historically, excess water from the C-23 Canal was routed toward the South Fork of the St. Lucie River, and those freshwater flows disrupted the estuary's natural salinity balance while carrying nutrients that contribute to algae growth.

The St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon suffered widespread toxic algae outbreaks in 2016 and 2018. The blooms damaged wildlife habitat, hurt local businesses and kept residents away from affected waterways. Newton Cook, who lives in Tequesta near the Indian River Lagoon, said clean water is good for the community. Cook said there has been a tremendous improvement in the water in different areas but there is still a long way to go.

The project is part of a broader network of restoration efforts involving the St. Lucie River, Indian River Lagoon and Everglades. DeSantis said Florida has committed nearly $10 billion to Everglades restoration and water quality projects since he took office in 2019. His administration has completed or begun work on more than 90 Everglades-related projects. DeSantis said a state and federal agreement is expected to accelerate completion of the Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee from 2034 to 2029. Once completed, the EAA reservoir is designed to store water from Lake Okeechobee, clean it and send it south toward the Everglades and Florida Bay rather than releasing it east into the St. Lucie River or west into the Caloosahatchee River.

cards.headline: DeSantis touts nearly $10 billion Everglades investment at Martin County C-23 project ribbon-cutting
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project, citing pump capacity that can fill an Olympic pool in under six minutes and projected reductions of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen annually.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, announcing his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019. DeSantis said the nearly $10 billion figure has never been matched in state history and includes more than 90 Everglades projects completed or broken ground on during his tenure.

The project at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River through a nearly seven-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water annually. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under six minutes.

South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett said the pump station is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day, comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system, and has been operational since May 14. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. Lambert said seagrass has returned to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary since DeSantis took office, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry.

DeSantis highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert, Bartlett, and South Florida Water Management District board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.

DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested for tracking ex-girlfriend 400 times via police databases
hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield faces four felonies after allegedly misusing police databases more than 400 times to track an ex-girlfriend from October 2022 to July 2023. Crutchfield is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond.

Fort Pierce police Chief David Smith confirmed Tuesday that Crutchfield conducted 382 searches using Flock cameras and additional queries through three other police databases to monitor a single vehicle registered to his ex-girlfriend. Smith said most of the queries were made when Crutchfield was off duty.

"Conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach in the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. The police chief called the arrest a difficult moment for the department but emphasized investigators acted on their obligation when credible evidence of wrongdoing emerged. "The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," Smith said.

Crutchfield resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department in August shortly after learning he was under investigation, according to Smith. The police chief announced the department is implementing new access restrictions for police databases, limiting who can use them and requiring permission from a deputy chief for all searches.

Smith called the arrest "a black eye" for the department but said investigators did what had to be done. "When there is credible evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act," Smith said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County advances bulk water agreement for P1 Motor Club racetrack
cards.teaser: Commissioners agreed to move forward with a bulk water service agreement for the proposed 650-acre motorsports development west of Port St. Lucie while directing staff to review utility policies over the next year.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners reached a consensus Tuesday to move forward with a bulk water service agreement for the proposed P1 Motor Club while directing staff to review the county's broader utility policies over the next year. The discussion came during the Board of County Commissioners' Sept. 8 informal meeting, where commissioners considered how the St. Lucie County Water and Sewer District should calculate water capacity for the motorsports-focused project planned on a 650-acre former citrus grove west of Port St. Lucie.

County staff said Phase 1 had been calculated at 126 equivalent residential connections, or ERCs, under the district's current methodology. P1 representatives argued the project's water demand should be lower than a traditional residential development because its garage-townhome units are intended for occasional or seasonal use. Staff said the units are built to residential standards, with kitchens and living areas, and that the district must reserve enough capacity to protect the utility system.

Commissioners agreed to pursue a bulk water agreement using the current ERC methodology to determine the project's daily water allocation. The agreement would allow P1 to manage water distribution within the project while the county retains safeguards for the utility system. The board also directed staff to begin a formal review of the county's Uniform Extension Policy and other utility-service standards, including whether bulk agreements or alternative calculation methods should be addressed for specialized developments. Staff was asked to complete that policy work within a year.

The private, members-only development is planned to include two racetracks, 125 condos and custom garages. The P1 website describes plans for more than nine miles of private track space, including a 4.5-mile P1 Circuit and a 3-mile Treasure Coast Circuit, as well as karting, rally and drift courses. The proposed development also includes trackside residences, garage townhomes, a clubhouse, event space and a motorsports-related commerce park. The site advertises its garage townhomes with full kitchens, living and dining areas, along with unlimited overnight stays for owners, families and guests.

The P1 discussion was the final major item during the nearly five-hour informal meeting. Earlier, commissioners discussed right-of-way needs and property acquisition for the estimated $30 million Selvitz Road widening project. The board asked staff to return with an update in February. Commissioners also reviewed possible changes to the use of a portion of the county's tourist development tax, received an update on efforts to address derelict vessels and long-term anchoring, and discussed potential expansions of permitted uses in agricultural zoning districts.

cards.headline: Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie moves forward with 60% of first retail phase already leased
cards.teaser: Developer Gustavo Lumer says construction on the first 40,000-square-foot parcel of the 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District could begin within six months, with 60 percent of the retail and restaurant space already leased.
cards.body:
Construction on the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie could begin within six months, with 60 percent of the initial retail and restaurant space already leased, according to developer Gustavo Lumer.

Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, said development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way that will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. The nearly 85-acre entertainment district is planned along Village Parkway in the Tradition community, divided between four parcels from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive.

"The retailers are eager to open yesterday. If we could pop it up next week and have it there, they're ready to go," Lumer said.

Lumer said he hopes to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south near the new Stars and Stripes Park. That section would serve as the hub of the entertainment district, with plans that include potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

"There's a need for diversity, and they keep telling us that they want different options," Lumer said.

Lumer said the district will be designed so visitors can park or arrive by golf cart and spend the afternoon moving between venues. Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often, while neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need.

"We need more places for people to go on a regular basis to intermingle," Gramata said.

Lumer said developers are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites. He said the district will help keep and attract business in Port St. Lucie.

"The more brands that they keep opening, everybody's realizing, well, I'm the only one missing out, and so you'll see a lot of beautiful brands coming in a short, short time," Lumer said.

hero.headline: C-23 Canal Diversion Project in Palm City now complete, has diverted 5 billion gallons since May
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the $57 million C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Palm City, which has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary since entering operational testing in May. The project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River each year on average, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water annually from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.

The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, reroutes excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. Previously, water from the C-23 Canal had contributed to harmful algal blooms in the estuary. The pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes when operating at full capacity.

Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said preventing these harmful discharges will improve the health of the estuary and the Indian River Lagoon. She said seagrass has returned to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary since DeSantis took office, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife.

South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett said the pump station is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert, Bartlett, and district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 and has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested on felony charges for tracking ex-girlfriend
hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond after being charged with four felonies for allegedly misusing police databases to track an ex-girlfriend. Fort Pierce police Chief David Smith announced the arrest Tuesday and detailed how the department is tightening access to surveillance databases in response.

Crutchfield conducted more than 400 searches from October 2022 to July 2023 to monitor a single vehicle registered to an ex-girlfriend, according to Chief Smith. Crutchfield used Flock cameras 382 times and accessed three other police databases, mostly while off duty. The Flock camera searches allowed him to track the victim's location and movements.

"Conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach in the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. Crutchfield resigned from the department in August shortly after learning he was under investigation.

Smith called the arrest "a black eye" for the department but said investigators had an obligation to act. "When there is credible evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," he said.

Smith announced changes to department policies regarding police database access. The new policies limit who can access the databases and require permission from a deputy chief for all searches. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community," Smith said.

hero.headline: Florida Realtors puts $10 million behind Amendment 3 as opponents warn of service cuts
hero.body:
Florida Realtors is investing $10 million to promote Amendment 3, a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%.

Margy Grant, CEO of Florida Realtors, said the campaign centers on helping families afford the ongoing costs of homeownership beyond the initial purchase. "Affordability doesn't end at closing. There's lots of costs that go into homeownership. For example, insurance, repairs, property taxes," Grant said. She said the changes would help homeowners retain more of their earnings and give rental and commercial property owners more predictability.

The state's Revenue Estimating Conference projects the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion if approved. The estimated losses begin at roughly $4.93 billion in fiscal year 2027–28 and grow over time. Opponents argue those losses could force cuts to services, higher fees or additional assessments. "You might pay a couple of thousand dollars less for your property taxes, but you're going to wind up paying more as the cost shifts onto fees, additional assessments," said Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on Amendment 3.

Cities, counties and public-safety groups opposing the amendment warn the losses could force difficult choices. "Are you going to have to pay a fee to use your local library? What about fire assessment fees, storm water, additional storm water fees?" Ousley said. Grant said the impact would vary across Florida's 67 counties and expressed confidence that local officials could make decisions to manage it. Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he will help promote the amendment in some capacity, despite wanting a larger property-tax cut.

An Aug. 18 Sachs Media survey of 800 Florida voters found 63% support overall and 37% opposition. That puts support three percentage points above the 60% required for passage, within the survey's overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Voters will decide Nov. 3.

hero.body:
Former Fort Pierce police officer Josepher Crutchfield is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond after being charged with four felonies for allegedly misusing police databases to track an ex-girlfriend. Fort Pierce police Chief David Smith announced Tuesday that the department has also imposed new access restrictions on police databases in response to the case.

Crutchfield used four different police databases to monitor a single vehicle from October 2022 to July 2023, Smith said. The registered owner of that vehicle was an ex-girlfriend. Crutchfield conducted more than 400 searches, using Flock cameras 382 times to track the victim's location and movements. Most of the queries were made when he was off duty.

"Conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach in the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. Crutchfield resigned from the department in August shortly after learning he was under investigation. Smith called the arrest "a black eye" for the department but emphasized investigators did what had to be done.

"When there is credible evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," Smith said. The chief announced changes to department policies regarding police database access, limiting who can access them and requiring permission from a deputy chief for all searches. Smith described the case as a difficult moment for the organization and the community.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access after stalking case
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer search license plates through the department's Flock camera system without approval from one of two deputy chiefs. Chief David Smith announced the new restrictions this week after former officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times.

Under the new rules, only lieutenants and higher-ranking officers can access the license plate reader system. Every search requires sign-off from a deputy chief and must be tied to a case number. The system can only be used to investigate forcible felonies as defined under Florida law and cases involving missing or endangered people. Camera records are now deleted after seven days instead of 30.

Before the changes, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith said the lieutenant-only access and deputy chief approval rules were added after the Crutchfield investigation began in August, though he had already started a one-year audit of database usage after becoming chief in February. Smith declined to give a specific date for when earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Investigators say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. He also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

Smith created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use. The department is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said Fort Pierce will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads.
hero.article_text: Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. While some people who spoke to CBS12 News are happy about the changes, some say they're conflicted about Flock camera use at all. You know, we do have we do have our own rights, you know, and all this data collection and everything else is definitely infringing upon that. On the other side of it, it is a great tool for law enforcement," said Edward Smith. "I think it's a good thing that they crack down on it. Like, you don't have to have it. You know, I don't need a camera watching me walk into the bathroom." Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.
