cards.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer who tracked ex with Flock cameras had 2021 sexual harassment suspension
cards.teaser: Josepher Crutchfield, arrested this week for allegedly accessing Flock and other databases 382 times to track his ex-girlfriend, was suspended for two days in 2021 after an internal affairs investigation found he sexually harassed female Fort Pierce police employees.
cards.body:
A former Fort Pierce police officer arrested this week for allegedly using law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend had previously been suspended for sexually harassing female employees in 2021.

Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department ultimately found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay.

Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO. Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information, searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth.

The latest investigation began on Aug. 10, 2026 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 7, 2026 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. A criminal investigation began and Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief David Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. Fort Pierce police have tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days.

hero.headline: Martin County C-23 Canal project completed, diverts nearly 5 billion gallons
hero.body:
The C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County has been completed and is now diverting excess water away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.

Gov. Ron DeSantis celebrated the completion Wednesday at the project site at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway. The project reroutes water from the C-23 Canal through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area instead of sending it to the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River, where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.

Bartlett said the pump station at the project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is part of a deeply interconnected system and preventing harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon. She pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 and has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects. He highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay.

hero.headline: Jet Ride Boat Club ceases operations, leaving Treasure Coast members without refunds
hero.body:
Jet Ride Boat Club ceased operations effective Sept. 1, citing rising costs and weather disruptions, leaving Treasure Coast members without refunds or boat access. A member provided an email from Jet Ride announcing the closure and suspension of month-to-month payments.

Member Obymachow said he is frustrated about the money he already paid. "I pay money, and then all of a sudden, without warning, it's just — it feels like a big slap in the face," Obymachow said. "Just so painful, you're like so accustomed to having a boat all the time you can use to now just having none."

Members of the Carefree Boat Club of the Treasure Coast received a similar email saying that club is also ceasing operations.

The original founder of Carefree Clubs of St. Augustine and Amelia Island sent members an email asking them to take a survey about whether the founder should step back in and rebuild the club.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access after ex-officer charged with stalking misuse
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run license plates through the department's Flock camera system on their own. Chief David Smith rolled out new restrictions this week after former officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. Every use now requires sign-off from one of two deputy chiefs, and only lieutenants and above can access the system at all.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

Under the new rules, every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly.

Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. The department is now deleting Flock camera records after 7 days instead of 30. Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began.

Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. The department is also pulling cameras off the road to comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. Smith estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads.

cards.headline: Judge denies bond reduction for ex-Fort Pierce officer accused of tracking ex-girlfriend
cards.teaser: A judge denied a request to lower the $80,000 bond for Josepher Crutchfield, who faces four felony counts for allegedly using law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend more than 400 times.
cards.body:
A judge denied a bond reduction request this morning for a former Fort Pierce police officer accused of misusing law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend, keeping his bond at $80,000. Josepher Crutchfield appeared at his first court appearance facing four third-degree felony counts, each carrying a $20,000 warrant.

Crutchfield's attorney asked the judge to reduce his bond, but the state argued the bond should remain in place, citing concerns about public trust in Flock cameras, a tool used by law enforcement to track vehicles. An assistant state attorney told the court that law enforcement officers entrusted with these duties should be the first not to abuse them, particularly given national concerns about Flock cameras.

Police said Crutchfield used Flock cameras and other law enforcement databases more than 400 times to track his ex-girlfriend's car, with 382 of those searches conducted through Flock cameras. Authorities said most of the searches occurred while Crutchfield was off duty, allowing him to see where and when her car was spotted.

Crutchfield resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month after learning he was under investigation. His bond remains set at $80,000.

cards.headline: Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie 60% pre-leased, construction to start within six months
cards.teaser: The first phase of the 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District along Village Parkway is 60 percent pre-leased and could begin construction within six months, with a larger entertainment hub planned near Stars and Stripes Park.
cards.body:
The nearly 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District planned along Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie has pre-leased 60 percent of its first retail and restaurant parcel, with construction expected to start within six months, according to developer Gustavo Lumer.

Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, said the initial development will cover a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way and will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. The development is divided among four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive.

Lumer said he plans to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The second phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the hub of the entertainment district, with plans for potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

Lumer said retailers are eager to open as soon as possible. Neighbors in the area welcomed the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often, while neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need for places where people can intermingle on a regular basis. Lumer said the development team is still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

hero.headline: Nearly 7-mile canal system in Palm City now diverts billions of gallons from St. Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
A new water-management project in Palm City is redirecting billions of gallons of water away from the St. Lucie Estuary to reduce the risk of harmful algal blooms in Martin County. The C-23 Estuary Discharge Diversion Project, which includes nearly seven miles of new canal and a pump station, entered operational testing in May and has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water. The system is projected to prevent an average of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the river each year.

Ron DeSantis joined state environmental officials in Palm City on Wednesday to mark the completion of the project. The pump station redirects excess water from the C-23 Canal to the C-44 reservoir and stormwater treatment area, where the water can be stored and cleaned instead of flowing directly into the St. Lucie Estuary. Drew Bartlett, executive director of the South Florida Water Management District, said the pump station can move as much as 166 million gallons of water per day.

Historically, excess water from the C-23 Canal was routed toward the South Fork of the St. Lucie River. Those freshwater flows can disrupt the estuary's natural salinity balance while carrying nutrients that contribute to algae growth. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the completed project is expected to divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the St. Lucie River.

The St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon suffered widespread toxic algae outbreaks in 2016 and 2018. The blooms damaged wildlife habitat, hurt local businesses and kept residents away from affected waterways. DeSantis said a more natural salinity gradient and better conditions for the estuary will produce better results for residents, for visitors, and for business owners all along the Indian River Lagoon.

The project is part of a broader network of restoration efforts involving the St. Lucie River, Indian River Lagoon and Everglades. The South Florida Water Management District and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also recently marked the completion of construction on the C-23/C-24 Stormwater Treatment Area, which is designed to remove nutrients from water before it reaches the estuary and southern Indian River Lagoon. DeSantis said Florida has committed nearly $10 billion to Everglades restoration and water-quality projects since he took office in 2019.

cards.headline: Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo's animal cruelty trial delayed to 2027
cards.teaser: The trial for Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo has been pushed to 2027 after at least a ninth continuance, with a key state witness on medical disability unable to testify until late January. The defense has also filed a motion to dismiss the case entirely.
cards.body:
The trial for Palm City dog trainer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo has been delayed until 2027, marking at least the ninth continuance in a case that began more than two years ago. In court Wednesday morning, prosecutor Kristin Chase told Judge Elizabeth Metzger that one of the state's key witnesses is on medical disability and cannot testify until at least the end of January, according to doctors. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be allowed to take the stand at trial. Metzger is now aiming for February for that hearing, pushing any potential trial date even further back.

Camerlengo faces two counts of animal cruelty in the deaths of two dogs that died while in the care of her Palm City training and boarding facility, Pawsitively Paradise. She was arrested in 2024 after Martin County detectives said the dogs died in her care. A WPTV investigation linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to Pawsitively Paradise over the course of a decade.

Her attorneys filed a motion to dismiss the case on Sept. 2, and Metzger ordered both sides to set a hearing on that motion by the end of this week. Camerlengo's next court date is set for December, though the judge could take up the motion to dismiss sooner. Defense attorney Stuart Kaplan has asked the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi. Kaplan told WPTV he believes the detective did not have all of the facts. The hearing to decide whether those witnesses can testify has not yet taken place.

The latest delay comes after a contentious July 2026 hearing in which Metzger pressed both the prosecution and defense over why the case still hadn't gone to trial. At one point, an exchange between Metzger and Kaplan grew heated. At that hearing, Metzger said the case had been continued so many times she had lost count.

For Adele Kirk Csontos, the wait for justice started even before Camerlengo's arrest. She filed a police report after her dog, Mako, died following 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Camerlengo was never charged in Mako's death because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs concluded they died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest and charges. Kirk Csontos said she did not think it would be two years. Despite the ongoing delays, Kirk Csontos said she is still hopeful that Camerlengo will be held accountable.

hero.headline: C-23 Canal diversion project in Martin County complete, rerouting billions of gallons from St. Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. history. The project will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River and send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.

Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. The pump station is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.

Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. The project is located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway and addresses excess water that had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms in the river.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019. cards.headline: Florida Realtors puts $10 million behind Amendment 3 property-tax cuts
cards.teaser: Florida Realtors is funding a $10 million campaign to support Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The state projects the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion.
cards.body:
Florida Realtors is putting $10 million behind a campaign to pass Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%.

Margy Grant, CEO of Florida Realtors, said the changes would help homeowners retain more of their earnings. The campaign centers on the argument that buying a home is only part of the affordability challenge and families need help paying to keep it. Grant said Amendment 3 provides the opportunity for homeowners to receive money they have earned and keep more of it.

The state's Revenue Estimating Conference projects that the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion if approved. The estimated losses begin at roughly $4.93 billion in fiscal year 2027–28 and grow over time. Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on Amendment 3, warned that residents might pay a couple of thousand dollars less for property taxes but wind up paying more as costs shift onto fees and additional assessments. Cities, counties and public-safety groups opposing the amendment warn that losses could force cuts to services, higher fees or additional assessments.

An Aug. 18 Sachs Media survey of 800 Florida voters found 63% support overall and 37% opposition. That puts support three percentage points above the 60% required for passage, within the survey's overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he will help promote the amendment in some capacity, despite wanting a larger property-tax cut. Voters will decide Nov. 3.

Families also need help paying to keep it."Affordability doesn't end at closing. There's lots of costs that go into homeownership. For example, insurance, repairs, property taxes," said Margy Grant, CEO of Florida Realtors.Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. The larger exemption would reduce the value of qualifying homes subject to those taxes.The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%. That cap applies to assessed values used to calculate taxes; local tax rates could still change.Grant said the changes would help homeowners retain more of their earnings and give rental and commercial property owners more predictability."Amendment 3 provides the opportunity for homeowners to literally receive money that they've earned and keep more of it," she said.The campaign arrives as Gov. What about fire assessment fees, storm water, additional storm water fees?" hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access to top brass after Crutchfield arrest
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer search license plates through the department's Flock camera system without approval from one of two deputy chiefs, and only lieutenants and above may access the system at all. Chief David Smith announced the restrictions this week after the arrest of former officer Josepher Crutchfield, who is accused of searching for a woman he once dated 382 times through the system.

Under the new rules, every search requires a case number and deputy chief sign off. The system may be used only for investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law and cases involving missing or endangered people. Smith also cut data retention from 30 days to seven days. Before the changes, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly.

Smith created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of every law enforcement database officers use. He said he began reviewing technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already started a one-year audit of database usage before media brought the allegations against Crutchfield to the department in August. The deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began, roughly two months ago.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

The new rules arrive as Fort Pierce is also removing cameras from the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights of way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. Smith said the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit and run that seriously injured a seven year old girl.
hero.article_text: Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. While some people who spoke to CBS12 News are happy about the changes, some say they're conflicted about Flock camera use at all. You know, we do have we do have our own rights, you know, and all this data collection and everything else is definitely infringing upon that. On the other side of it, it is a great tool for law enforcement," said Edward Smith. "I think it's a good thing that they crack down on it. Like, you don't have to have it. You know, I don't need a camera watching me walk into the bathroom." Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.

hero.headline: Martin County C-23 Canal project diverts nearly 5 billion gallons from Saint Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
The C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary since entering its operational testing phase in May. Gov. Ron DeSantis celebrated completion of the project on Wednesday at the site on Southwest Martin Highway.

The project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, according to Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert. The pump station can move 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14.

The project reroutes excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. The water previously contributed to harmful algal blooms in the estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.

Lambert said the project will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert, South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, and district board members including Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019. He said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. The governor cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments.

Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife.

hero.headline: Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie to break ground within six months
hero.body:
Construction on the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie is expected to begin within six months, with 60 percent of the initial 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space already leased. The nearly 85-acre development along Village Parkway in the Tradition community is moving forward faster than anticipated, according to developer Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate.

The entertainment district is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include the 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said the retailers are eager to open as soon as possible.

Lumer plans to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. This section would serve as the hub of the entertainment district and includes plans for potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

Lumer said the district will be a place where residents can park or arrive by golf cart and spend the afternoon visiting different establishments. Neighbors in the area have welcomed the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often, while neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need for places where people can gather regularly. Lumer said developers are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access after ex-officer's 382 searches
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer search license plates through the department's Flock camera system without approval from one of two deputy chiefs, part of sweeping new restrictions Chief David Smith announced this week after a former officer was arrested for allegedly using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all, every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people.

Before the changes, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. The department is also deleting Flock camera records after 7 days instead of 30.

"The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient."

Former officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began.

Under the new process, if detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. If they receive approval, the lieutenant conducts the query using a case number specifically tied to an investigation.

"The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said.

Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use. The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far.

The department is also pulling cameras off the road in response to a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights of way. Smith estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads.
hero.article_text: Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.

cards.headline: Man shoots aggressive dog in Indian River Estates after wife trapped in car
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed a man shot one of two dogs that approached his wife's vehicle and prevented her from exiting, then charged at him in the Indian River Estates subdivision.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office on Monday confirmed a man shot one of two dogs that behaved aggressively and trapped his wife in her vehicle in the Indian River Estates subdivision.

The incident occurred Sunday in the 5900 block of Palm Drive. The man's wife pulled into her driveway when two dogs approached her vehicle and prevented her from safely getting out. She contacted her husband for assistance. He came outside and observed the dogs before returning inside the residence to retrieve a handgun.

When the man came back outside, one dog charged toward him in an aggressive manner, the sheriff's office said. He fired his handgun and struck one of the dogs as it approached and before he was bitten.

Both dogs fled to a nearby residence on Myrtle Drive, where they reside. The owner took the injured dog to an emergency animal hospital for treatment, and the dog needed surgery. Detectives with the Criminal Investigations Division reviewed available surveillance footage and conducted interviews. The sheriff's office submitted a request to Animal Control for follow-up investigation.

After the incident Sunday in the 5900 block of Palm Drive, detectives with the Criminal Investigations Division reviewed available surveillance footage and conducted interviews. "Investigators confirmed that two dogs were behaving aggressively and attempting to attack family members," the agency posted on Facebook. The man's wife pulled into her driveway, and two dogs approached her vehicle and prevented her from safely getting out of her vehicle. She contacted her husband for assistance. He said he came outside and observed the dogs before returning inside the residence to retrieve a handgun. When he came back outside, one dog charged toward him in an aggressive manner, the sheriff's office said. As the dog approached and before he was bitten, the man fired his handgun, striking one of the dogs. After the shooting, both dogs fled to a nearby residence on Myrtle Drive, where they reside. The owner took the injured dog to an emergency animal hospital for treatment, and the dog needed surgery. "At this time, the status of the dog is unknown," the agency said. cards.headline: Fort Pierce police chief details 400+ database searches, new Flock policies after officer's arrest
cards.teaser: A former Fort Pierce police officer accessed law enforcement databases more than 400 times with no legitimate purpose, including 382 Flock searches of his ex-girlfriend's license plate, prompting sweeping new department restrictions.
cards.body:
A former Fort Pierce police officer accessed law enforcement databases more than 400 times with no legitimate purpose, including 382 Flock searches of his ex-girlfriend's license plate, prompting sweeping new department restrictions on the automated license plate reader system.

Josopher Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access after resigning from the Fort Pierce Police Department in August. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose, according to investigators. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. The investigation expanded to other databases including FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO, where investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information with no legitimate law enforcement purpose.

Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay. The latest investigation began Aug. 10 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave Aug. 7 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. He resigned Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed.

Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said the department has tightened access to the Flock system in response. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. The department added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases, and so far no additional violations have been identified.

Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access, according to the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes. Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC , NCIC , DAVID and TLO . Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information - searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth. Officers must acknowledge a warning each time they access the systems, confirming they are being used for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The chief said investigators are not speculating about Crutchfield's intentions or whether the alleged conduct amounted to stalking, but they will follow any additional leads. "The conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach of the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. " Again, it does not diminish the dedicated work that our officers do every day." The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases. So far, officials said no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have also tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," said Smith. Officials also added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. The chief acknowledged the incident is a setback for the department but said officials are committed to being transparent and holding officers accountable. "This is a black eye for the agency," the chief said. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community, but our responsibility is clear. The authority entrusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is criminal evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

cards.headline: Fort Pierce to remove roughly 50 Flock cameras from state and county roads
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police will remove approximately 50 automated license plate reader cameras from state and county rights of way following directives from the Florida Department of Transportation and St. Lucie County Commission.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police announced Tuesday they are preparing to remove approximately 50 Flock automated license plate reader cameras from state and county rights of way following recent directives from the Florida Department of Transportation and St. Lucie County Commission, Police Chief David Smith said.

The disclosure came during a news conference where Smith announced the arrest of former Fort Pierce officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access. Investigators say Crutchfield used the Flock database 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026 to search the same vehicle license plate registered to his ex-girlfriend.

Smith defended the Flock technology as a valuable investigative tool when used appropriately, pointing to its use in homicide investigations and a hit-and-run involving a 7-year-old girl. The department has implemented new restrictions requiring prior approval from one of two deputy chiefs for Flock searches, with access limited to personnel at the rank of lieutenant or above.

Under the new policy, the technology may only be used for investigations involving forcible felonies or missing and endangered people, and every search must be connected to a case number. The department also reduced its data retention period from 30 days to seven days.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 secured bond. The investigation began after members of the media contacted the department on Aug. 7 with information raising concerns about Crutchfield's possible misuse of the Flock system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave that same day and resigned from the department on Aug. 18.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested for tracking ex-girlfriend 382 times
hero.body:
A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts after investigators say he accessed Flock license plate readers and other law enforcement databases 382 times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department in August and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond.

Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose, according to the department. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO, where investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information with no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth.

The investigation began Aug. 10 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave Aug. 7 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. He resigned Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes.

Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases, and so far no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have tightened access to the Flock system so only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days and added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases.

Crutchfield previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. The department found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay.

cards.teaser: Fort Pierce Police Chief David M. Smith on Tuesday laid out how a media inquiry on Aug. 7 led to the arrest of former officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce Police Chief David M. Smith on Tuesday detailed the timeline that led from a media inquiry to the arrest of former police officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access.

Smith said the investigation began Aug. 7 following an inquiry by the media about possible misuse of the license plate reader system. Later that day, Smith placed Crutchfield on administrative leave and immediately revoked his access to all law enforcement systems. By Aug. 10, Fort Pierce Police Department investigators developed additional information to begin a criminal investigation. The investigation was conducted by police department detectives in consultation with the State Attorney's Office of the 19th Judicial Circuit, which includes St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Crutchfield submitted his resignation Aug. 18 before the case was resolved. The investigation established probable cause that a crime was committed, and Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday, Sept. 8.

Smith said the investigation revealed that between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield accessed the Flock database 382 times to search for the same vehicle license plate using multiple different reason categories for why the license plate was being searched. The searches did not have any meaningful law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while Crutchfield was off duty. The investigation revealed that the registered owner of the vehicle was Crutchfield's former girlfriend.

Smith said once the misuse of the Flock camera database was discovered, the review was expanded to other law enforcement databases. Crutchfield allegedly accessed NCIC, the DAVID, and TLO databases for the same license plate number of his former girlfriend. Those searches also did not have meaningful law enforcement use. The databases store information for legitimate law-enforcement purposes and access is not provided for personal use. Smith said Crutchfield is in the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 bail. Smith said during the press conference that the badge does not provide immunity from accountability.

hero.headline: Former NYPD Ground Zero responder Frank Frangella leads Martin County school safety
hero.body:
Frank Frangella spent weeks digging through rubble at Ground Zero after the September 11 attacks. Now he leads safety and security for all Martin County schools and says he has not forgotten a single moment.

Frangella's office serves as a quiet tribute to that day. Photos, statues, and mementos fill the space, each one tied to his time working at Ground Zero in the weeks and months following the attacks. Among them is a memory book, photos of his team, images of mountains of debris and twisted metal, and pictures of celebrities who brought hot meals to first responders.

One photo stands out above the rest, filled with circular light reflections that Frangella likes to think of as the ascending souls of those lost that day.

For Frangella, the phrase "never forget" carries a meaning that extends well beyond September 11, 2001. "That it happened, that we acknowledge that it happened and the lives that were lost," Frangella said. "Not only on that day, but for the last 25 years. Everybody else that unfortunately passed away from illnesses of being down there."

Frangella now calls Martin County home. He said he cannot bring himself to return to the 9/11 museum and memorial in New York City, saying it would be too painful.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Carefree Boat Club location goes dark, leaving members unable to reach staff or make reservations
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce location of Carefree Boat Club of Treasure Coast has gone dark, with an empty office, no staff available, and no way for members to make reservations, leaving paying members with limited options and unanswered questions.

Peter Terry, who moved to Fort Pierce from Maryland, paid a $3,000 initiation fee plus monthly membership and reservation fees to access rental boats at the Fort Pierce location. More than a month ago, Terry noticed the office was empty and he could no longer make reservations. Terry said he has received no communication from the local franchise and there is nobody to call.

Carefree Boat Club Network LLC, the corporate office, told WPTV through its attorneys that each club operates independently and is responsible for its own day-to-day operations, staffing, and finances. The company said its shared reservation platform remains operational, and members whose local club has closed or suspended operations can continue to book at other club locations subject to availability and hosting club policies. The attorneys said questions regarding initiation fees, membership dues, or other charges specific to a member's local club should be directed to that club directly, as those matters are governed by the member's agreement with the local licensee, not with the corporate network office.

With no option in Fort Pierce, Terry can only use the Vero Beach and Stuart locations. WPTV called the number on the Carefree Boat Club of Treasure Coast website multiple times with no answer. WPTV also reached out to the phone number on the outside of the Fort Pierce location office with no answer. Calls to the dock phone for both the Stuart and Vero Beach locations went unanswered, and a message indicated the mailbox was full.

Terry said his expectations were that the Fort Pierce center would be maintained in an appropriate manner. He said he had a certain set of expectations going into the transaction, and those expectations have not been met, leaving him annoyed and disappointed.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested on felony charges for tracking ex-girlfriend
hero.body:
A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access after authorities say he used a license plate reader database 382 times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield faces charges following an investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department and the State Attorney's Office of the 19th Judicial Circuit.

Fort Pierce Police Chief David M. Smith announced the arrest during a press conference on September 8. Smith said the investigation revealed Crutchfield accessed the Flock automated License Plate Reader database between October 2025 and July 2026 to search for the same vehicle license plate using multiple different reason categories. The searches did not have any meaningful law enforcement purpose, and most were made while Crutchfield was off duty. The registered owner of the vehicle was Crutchfield's former girlfriend.

The investigation began on August 7 following a media inquiry about possible misuse of the license plate reader system. Smith placed Crutchfield on administrative leave that day and immediately revoked his access to all law enforcement systems. By August 10, investigators developed additional information to begin a criminal investigation. Crutchfield submitted his resignation on August 18, before the case was resolved.

The investigation also revealed Crutchfield accessed NCIC, DAVID, and TLO databases for the same license plate number. Those searches also did not have meaningful law enforcement use. The databases store information for legitimate law enforcement purposes and access is not provided for personal use. Crutchfield is being held in the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 bail. The State Attorney's Office of the 19th Judicial Circuit, which includes St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties, consulted on the investigation.

Smith addressed the arrest directly during the press conference. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community," Smith said. "But our responsibility is clear. The authority trusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is credible evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested for tracking ex-girlfriend with police database
hero.body:
A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts after investigators say he repeatedly accessed law enforcement databases without a legitimate police purpose, including 382 searches involving a vehicle registered to his ex-girlfriend. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith announced a comprehensive policy overhaul in response to the case, including restricted Flock access, shorter data retention, a new audit position, and removal of approximately 50 cameras from public rights of way.

Former Officer Josepher Crutchfield was being held Tuesday at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 secured bond. Smith said the investigation began after members of the media contacted the department on Aug. 7 with information raising concerns about Crutchfield's possible misuse of the department's Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave that same day and immediately lost access to law enforcement systems. Police launched a criminal investigation by Aug. 10 in consultation with the State Attorney's Office. Crutchfield resigned from the department on Aug. 18, before the investigation was completed.

Investigators found that between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly used the Flock database 382 times to search the same vehicle license plate. Police said Crutchfield used multiple reason categories to justify the searches, but investigators found no legitimate law enforcement purpose for them. Most of these queries were made while he was off duty, Smith said. Records from other law enforcement databases showed Crutchfield's access involving the woman stretched back to 2023, although the Flock searches began in October 2025. When a reporter asked whether Crutchfield appeared to be tracking his ex-girlfriend, Smith said he would not speculate about Crutchfield's intentions, but added, "I think you can infer that he was tracking an ex-girlfriend." The woman whose information was accessed has been notified and is part of the case.

After discovering the Flock searches, investigators expanded their review to other law enforcement databases, including FCIC/NCIC, DAVID and TLO. Police said they identified additional searches involving the same license plate that had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. The four databases are tied to the four felony charges Crutchfield now faces. Officers are shown a warning each time they access the databases and must acknowledge that the information is being accessed for a legitimate law enforcement purpose, Smith said. The warning also advises users that misuse could result in loss of access, disciplinary action or criminal charges.

Smith announced several changes to how Fort Pierce police can use automated license plate reader technology. Under the new restrictions, Flock searches require prior approval from one of the department's two deputy chiefs, and access is limited to personnel at the rank of lieutenant or above. The technology may now only be used for investigations involving forcible felonies or missing and endangered people, and every search must be connected to a case number. The department also reduced its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. The Fort Pierce Police Department added a position within its Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality-assurance audits of law enforcement database use. Smith said the department has also launched a comprehensive audit of its employees' use of law enforcement databases. As of Tuesday afternoon, he said no additional violations had been identified.

Fort Pierce police are also preparing to remove approximately 50 Flock cameras from state and county rights of way following recent directives from the Florida Department of Transportation and St. Lucie County Commission. Smith defended the technology as a valuable investigative tool when used appropriately, pointing to its use in homicide investigations and a hit-and-run involving a 7-year-old girl. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who are entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. "This is a black eye for the agency, we know that," Smith said. "But we're still standing here in front of you being transparent about what occurred." Smith said the case should demonstrate that officers who misuse law enforcement systems will be held accountable. "The badge does not provide immunity from accountability," Smith said.

cards.headline: 800 gallons of sewage spill at Port St. Lucie lift station after power failure
cards.teaser: A power failure at a Port St. Lucie lift station Tuesday morning caused about 800 gallons of untreated wastewater to spill onto a driveway and nearby swale. The city's monitoring system did not detect the outage.
cards.body:
About 800 gallons of untreated wastewater spilled from a Port St. Lucie lift station Tuesday after the station lost full electrical power, according to a pollution notice filed with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The city's SCADA monitoring system did not detect the issue.

Utility staff discovered sewage escaping from the wet well lid at the WP-22 lift station at 170 SW Hawthorne Circle at about 11 a.m. during weekly station checks, the notice said. The wastewater was flowing onto the station driveway and a nearby swale at an estimated rate of 10 gallons per minute.

Staff determined the station was not receiving full FPL line power, reported the outage and deployed a backup generator to restart the pumps. The spill stopped at about 12:20 p.m., the report said.

City staff estimated about 80 gallons, or 10 percent of the wastewater, soaked into the soil. A vacuum truck recovered about 720 gallons from the stone surface, grass and swale area, according to the notice. Workers disinfected the affected area with lime.

The report said no surface water or public-access areas were affected, and sampling was not required. Regulatory agencies and internal city notifications were underway, according to the report.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man found asleep in stolen car at Treasure Coast Square mall with stolen credit cards
cards.teaser: Martin County deputies arrested Cedric Lenard Culver after finding him sleeping in a stolen vehicle at Treasure Coast Square mall with multiple stolen credit cards and documents inside.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies arrested 18-year-old Cedric Lenard Culver of Fort Pierce after finding him asleep in a stolen car at Treasure Coast Square mall with stolen credit cards and documents inside.

A search of the vehicle uncovered multiple stolen credit and bank cards along with personal information documents belonging to other people. Deputies are working with the Port St. Lucie Police Department to identify and locate the victims whose credit cards, personal documents, and vehicle were stolen. Investigators believe the stolen property may be connected to multiple burglaries in St. Lucie County.

Culver told deputies he had damaged the stolen vehicle after crashing into another car. He said he did not stop because he was afraid he would be caught driving a stolen vehicle. Culver was charged with grand theft auto and trafficking in or possession of stolen credit cards.

cards.headline: Tradition Entertainment District to break ground in six months on first phase
cards.teaser: Lumer Real Estate plans to develop an 85-acre entertainment district along Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie's Tradition community. Construction on the first 5.5-acre parcel is expected to start within six months, with 60 percent of that space already leased.
cards.body:
Lumer Real Estate plans to develop a nearly 85-acre entertainment district along Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie's Tradition community, with construction on the first phase expected to start within six months. Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, said 60 percent of the first parcel is already leased.

The Tradition Entertainment District is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Lumer said he hopes to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space.

"The retailers are eager to open yesterday. If we could pop it up next week and have it there, they're ready to go," Lumer said. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the hub of the entertainment district.

Plans include potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater. Lumer said the district will help keep and attract business in Port St. Lucie. Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often. Neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need. "We need more places for people to go on a regular basis to intermingle," Gramata said. Lumer said they are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

cards.headline: Man shoots dog during attack in Fort Pierce; Animal Control investigating
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce man shot one of two dogs that were acting aggressively and attacking family members in the Indian River Estates subdivision Sunday. The injured dog required surgery, and Animal Control is conducting a follow-up investigation.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce man shot one of two dogs that were acting aggressively and attacking family members in the Indian River Estates subdivision Sunday, and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has requested Animal Control conduct a follow-up investigation.

The incident occurred in the 5900 block of Palm Drive. Detectives with the Criminal Investigations Division reviewed available surveillance footage and conducted interviews after the shooting. The injured dog was taken to an emergency animal hospital for treatment and required surgery, according to the sheriff's office.

The man's wife pulled into her driveway, and two dogs approached her vehicle and prevented her from safely getting out. She contacted her husband for assistance. He came outside and observed the dogs before returning inside the residence to retrieve a handgun, the sheriff's office said.

When he came back outside, one dog charged toward him in an aggressive manner. As the dog approached and before he was bitten, the man fired his handgun, striking one of the dogs. After the shooting, both dogs fled to a nearby residence on Myrtle Drive, where they reside. The owner took the injured dog to an emergency animal hospital for treatment. The sheriff's office said the status of the dog is unknown. A request was submitted to Animal Control for follow-up investigation.

"Investigators confirmed that two dogs were behaving aggressively and attempting to attack family members," the agency posted on Facebook. The man's wife pulled into her driveway, and two dogs approached her vehicle and prevented her from safely getting out of her vehicle. She contacted her husband for assistance. He said he came outside and observed the dogs before returning inside the residence to retrieve a handgun. When he came back outside, one dog charged toward him in an aggressive manner, the sheriff's office said. The owner took the injured dog to an emergency animal hospital for treatment, and the dog needed surgery. "At this time, the status of the dog is unknown," the agency said. hero.headline: JetBlue ends Vero Beach to JFK route permanently after demand falls short
hero.body:
JetBlue will permanently end flights from Vero Beach Regional Airport to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport starting Wednesday, September 9. The airline said demand for the route has not materialized as the company had hoped. The cancellation comes less than a year after JetBlue began service at the airport and undercuts expansion plans that included about $5 million in construction projects for baggage claim and covered walkways tied to the new service.

JetBlue will continue to serve Vero Beach through Boston Logan International Airport. Customers who booked flights on the JFK route were notified directly and issued refunds to their original form of payment.

JetBlue announced in December 2025 it would begin serving Vero Beach Regional Airport with daily flights to both JFK and Boston. The airport expected the new service to bring an influx of passengers, prompting the terminal improvements.

The route cancellation comes as JetBlue adds eight new nonstop routes to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. In a statement obtained by CBS12 in July, the airline confirmed the Vero Beach to JFK route would end while maintaining the Boston service.

cards.headline: 85-acre entertainment district planned for Tradition in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A developer plans to bring roughly 25 restaurants and retailers to an 85-acre entertainment district along Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie's Tradition community, with the first phase already 60 percent leased.
cards.body:
A nearly 85-acre entertainment district is in the works in Port St. Lucie along Village Parkway in the Tradition community, with new restaurants and stores expected to arrive within six months.

Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, is behind the property that would become the Tradition Entertainment District. The development is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Lumer said he hopes to bring in around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area.

Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said 60 percent of that space is already leased, and he expects construction to start within six months. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the hub of the entertainment district. Plans include potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often. Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need. Lumer said the more brands that keep opening, the more other brands will follow. Lumer said the district will help keep and attract business in Port St. Lucie. Lumer said they are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.
